messages.subject: Stan with large data?
parts:
I have a data set with approximately 10e7 observations. My model ends up with less than 10e3 predictors, as I have three continuous predictors and then 3 categorical predictors which I am treating as modelled intercepts (lengths of 10, 50 and 833). I am running on one of the top AWS instances (over 250gb ram) and last night I left the model on and came back this morning to find it still sitting on 'now on chain 3'. I'm using PyStan, and my code is below. I guess my question is whether this is even going to be possible. Can Stan handle this size of model yet?

logit_code = """
data {
  int<lower=0> N; 
  int<lower=0> n_year; 
  int<lower=0> n_country; 
  int<lower=0> n_nace;  
  int<lower=1,upper=n_year> year[N];
  int<lower=1,upper=n_country> country[N];
  int<lower=1,upper=n_nace> nace[N];
  vector[N] assets;
  vector[N] turnover;
  vector<lower=0>[N] stock;
  int<lower=0,upper=1> y[N];
} 
parameters {
  vector[n_year] b_year;
  vector[n_country] b_country;
  vector[n_nace] b_nace;
  vector[4] beta;
  real mu;
  real mu_year;
  real mu_firm;
  real mu_country;
  real mu_nace;
  real<lower=0,upper=100> sigma_year;
  real<lower=0,upper=100> sigma_country;
  real<lower=0,upper=100> sigma_nace;
} 
transformed parameters {
  vector[N] y_hat;
  for (i in 1:N)
    y_hat[i] <- beta[1] + beta[2]*assets[i] + beta[3]*turnover[i] + beta[4]*stock[i] + b_year[year[i]] + b_country[country[i]] + b_nace[nace[i]];
}
model {  
  b_year ~ normal (0, sigma_year);
  b_country ~ normal (0, sigma_country);
  b_nace ~ normal (0, sigma_nace);
  beta ~ normal (0, 100);
  y ~ bernoulli_logit(y_hat);
}
"""
regress_dat = {
'N' : len(df),
'y' : df.onepat.tolist(),
'assets' : df.assets.tolist(),
'turnover' : df.turnover.tolist(),
'stock' : df.stock.tolist(),
'n_year' : len(pd.unique(df.year)),
'n_country' : len(pd.unique(df.country)),
'n_nace' : len(pd.unique(df.nace)),
'year' : year,
'country' : country,
'nace' : nace
}
fit = pystan.stan(model_code=logit_code, data=regress_dat, iter=25000, chains=4, n_jobs=4)

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Stan with large data?
parts:
People have reported success using models with this many predictors and models with this much data, although
the ultimate success will depend on your model.

Firstly, you need priors on the sigmas: uniform on [0,100] will not be sufficient for a reasonable fit.  We’ve had great success with the semi-informative priors implied by Cauchy(0, 2.5) to Cauchy(0, 5).  Secondly, a N(0, 100) prior on the slopes is pretty wide — do you really expect such extreme slopes?  Pushing down to something more reasonable, like N(0, 10) will speed up the fit dramatically.

You’ll also want to consider a non-centered parameterization — with this much data it’s not clear if it will be better a priori but it may yield a significant speed up.

But perhaps most importantly, why are you running so many iterations? Remember that HMC is much more efficient than conventional samplers, so if you only need a few hundred samples for reasonable expectation estimates you should only need a few hundred effective samples, which is typically given within a thousand or so HMC samples (maybe more if your model is particularly bad).  25,000 * 4 = 100,000 iterations would be far more than necessary.  Remember — raw iterations don’t matter, only effective sample size.

On Monday, August 18, 2014 2:34:38 AM UTC-4, Christopher Grainger wrote:
transformed parameters {
  vector[N] y_hat;
  for (i in 1:N)
    y_hat[i] <- beta[1] + beta[2]*assets[i] + beta[3]*turnover[i] + beta[4]*stock[i] + b_year[year[i]] + b_country[country[i]] + b_nace[nace[i]];
}
model {

Declaring and defining y_hat in transformed parameters means that the entire y_hat vector of length 10^7 gets stored every iteration, which slows things down and eats a lot of disk space and / or RAM with no real benefit in this case. So, you can just move all that to the top of the model block, in which case it will not be stored. Also, it is worthwhile to use matrix algebra for the common part of y_hat like

model {
  vector[N] y_hat;
  y_hat <- X * beta; # constant, assets, turnover, and stock
  for(i in 1:N) y_hat[i] <- y_hat[i] + b_year[year[i]] + b_country[country[i]] + b_nace[nace[i]];
  y ~ bernoulli_logit(y_hat);
  // priors
}

Ben
